title: Do big lever governmental decisions help learning happen or do they get in the way?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton considers whether government and state education decisions actually affect learning, concluding they mostly act on the factors around learning, such as budgets, buildings and curriculum, rather than on the messy process in classrooms. He contrasts big levers pulled by governments with little levers pulled by teachers, students and parents in thousands of rooms at once. The UK education bill, which he notes never mentions learning, and a friend's school facing closure show how decisions have residual emotional effects on staff, parents and students. He argues that big lever players owe little lever players the conditions to do their part, but also that educators should take responsibility for what they control. His own long career, he says, was shaped far more by daily classroom work than by policy. He previews the next phase of posts on students, parents, teachers and school leaders.
points: Governments pull big levers that reach the factors affecting learning, while learning itself is driven by little levers pulled locally in classrooms.
The UK education bill's press release talks of standards, costs and safeguarding, not student learning, which Skelton reads as realism about government's reach.
A school closure announcement shows how big decisions erode emotional resilience, focus and systematic rigour, which in turn affects learning.
He sets out a deal that big lever players should help little lever players do their part, while teachers should not let every external decision derail them.
The practical message is that schools have real agency and should concentrate on the small levers, with the US federal share of school influence cited as roughly ten per cent.
quotes: Once the big levers have been pulled at governmental or state level, matters are largely out of their hands. For the most part, they can’t get close to the little levers that are at the heart of the action.
The little levers that make the learning difference are being pulled simultaneously and differently in thousands of classrooms by thousands of students, teachers, school leaders and parents.

That probably isn’t because the government doesn’t care about improving student learning. It’s probably because the government realises that it can have an impact on some of the factors that affect learning but not on the actual processes that really make learning happen.

Much as some people would like it to be otherwise, they do have feelings, states of minds and dispositions that create feelings that are more or less helpful to learning. It’s just how it is, and sometimes these feelings make it very hard to ‘just get on with it.

There’s a deal to be made here. If the big lever players want the little lever players to successfully deliver their part in the process then the little lever players have a right to expect the big lever players to help them do so.
There is a comfort in this. We all have agency when we are pulling those levers which actually makes a real difference.
The challenge is for those of us in schools to take responsibility for learning. We don’t pull the big levers; we pull the little ones.
